clue.text: Fly back from deepest Estonia

indicators.note: going back means the run of letters is read from right to left
taken from inside the next words, so the letters sit across the word break

blocks.note: the tail of deepest runs straight into the start of Estonia

explanation.surface: A traveller remarks on an insect met in the remotest corners of Estonia.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the end of 'deepest' and the start of 'Estonia' backwards to get TSETSE.
explanation.definitionFit: The tsetse is an African biting insect that spreads sleeping sickness, an example of a fly.

clue.text: Tourist beginning to think it's great in Australia!

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

explanation.surface: A visitor's first thought on arriving Down Under is how wonderful it all is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ripper' is Australian slang meaning excellent or great, as in 'a ripper of a day'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tripper is someone on a day trip or short holiday, a synonym for a sightseer.

clue.text: Cockney believed Queen to be authority figure

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker famously drops the H at the start of words

blocks.note: Elizabeth Regina, the usual crossword queen

explanation.surface: A Londoner from the East End thought the monarch ought to be in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys from London's East End drop their aitches, so 'held' becomes 'eld.
explanation.definitionFit: An elder is a senior, respected member of a church or community who holds sway over it.

clue.text: Weather's not hot — put on second jumper

indicators.note: not means the letter standing for hot is taken away
in a down entry, one piece is placed on top of the next

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for a second
H for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: The weather has turned cool, so it is time to add another layer of knitwear.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's in 'Weather's' is just 'is'; once H leaves WEATHER, S goes on top. A jumper is the British word for a pullover sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a jumper is a knitted pullover, the same garment Americans call a sweater.

clue.text: Holy men are not commonly found in SS

indicators.note: what is found in something sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written; it wraps round the other piece
the colloquial contraction ain't, said commonly for are not

explanation.surface: A grim remark that no holy men served in the Nazi SS.
explanation.walkthrough: SS also abbreviates 'saints', which makes the surface neater than it looks.
explanation.definitionFit: Saints are people recognised as especially holy, and the clue's men just makes them plural.

clue.text: Letters from the late Jesse Owens, perhaps

indicators.note: the letters are taken from the words and rearranged to spell something new

explanation.surface: Correspondence left behind by the late Olympic sprinter Jesse Owens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' looks like correspondence but signals a rearrangement of the letters in 'the late'. Owens, who has died, fits 'the late' too.
explanation.definitionFit: Jesse Owens won four gold medals at the 1936 Olympics, an example of a track and field sportsman.

clue.text: Old trade union to run schools for tots

blocks.note: the National Union of Railwaymen, a former British union
a run of things, a series

explanation.surface: A defunct union decides to operate some preschool establishments.
explanation.walkthrough: The NUR was the National Union of Railwaymen, merged into the RMT in 1990.
explanation.definitionFit: Nurseries are preschools caring for very young children, which is what tots are.

clue.text: After end of recess, Attlee set out for US city

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, which alone is kept
things set out are laid out afresh, so these letters take a new order
one piece comes after the other in the answer

explanation.surface: When Parliament's recess ended, the British prime minister Attlee left for America.
explanation.walkthrough: Clement Attlee was Britain's postwar Labour prime minister; his name is only fodder here.
explanation.definitionFit: Seattle is the largest city in Washington state, in the Pacific Northwest of America.

clue.text: Looking for first slice of summer pudding

indicators.note: the first slice of a word is its opening letter alone

explanation.surface: Someone hunting for a portion of summer pudding, a British berry dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: Summer pudding is a British dessert of berries in bread. Afters is British slang for the dessert course, and pudding means any dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage both pudding and afters name the sweet course served at the end of a meal.

clue.text: Central reservation is not very exciting

blocks.note: first meaning: literally the centre strip of a dual carriageway
second meaning: moderate, unadventurous, appealing to the mainstream

explanation.surface: A grumble that the strip down the motorway is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: A central reservation is the British term for the median strip between the carriageways of a motorway.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally the median strip lies mid-carriageway; figuratively the phrase means bland, safe and mainstream.

clue.text: Whisky? It's vital!

blocks.note: first meaning: a distilled alcoholic drink
second meaning: the vital principle, the animating force of life

explanation.surface: A drinker insists that whisky is essential to life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vital' here keeps its root sense of life: the vital spirit animating the body.
explanation.definitionFit: Whisky is a spirit, a distilled liquor, and the spirit is the life force that keeps a body alive.

clue.text: Steelmen recast iron and carbon, perhaps

indicators.note: metal recast is melted and shaped anew, so these letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: Steelworkers melt down and recast the iron and carbon that make steel.
explanation.walkthrough: Steel is mostly iron alloyed with carbon, so the surface is a neat industrial picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron and carbon are chemical elements, examples of substances that cannot be broken down further.

clue.text: Book of the Bible turns out to be about king and rabbi, essentially

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its very centre, so the middle letter is kept
about means surrounding, so one piece goes round the others
joins two pieces side by side

blocks.note: something that turns out to be so proves to be so
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A book of scripture is said to be about a king and a Jewish teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: PROVES opens between E and S to take in R and B.
explanation.definitionFit: Proverbs is the Old Testament book of wise sayings traditionally attributed to King Solomon.

clue.text: Articulate poetry about exotic island

indicators.note: about means round, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: the Indonesian island, exotic as a holiday spot

explanation.surface: Someone eloquent writes poems about a far-off island paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articulate' reads as an adjective, but it is the verb meaning to put into words.
explanation.definitionFit: To articulate is to express in words, and to verbalise means the same thing.

clue.text: Former partner lied about being sent away

indicators.note: turned about means moved around, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: an ex is a former spouse or lover

explanation.surface: An ex-spouse lied about why they were banished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning' but asks for the letters of 'lied' to be reordered.
explanation.definitionFit: To be exiled is to be banished from one's country, forced to leave home.

clue.text: Tony's family heard noises

indicators.note: what is heard is judged by its sound, not its spelling

blocks.note: Tony Blair's family are the Blairs

explanation.surface: Tony's relatives picked up some sounds.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Blair was the British prime minister from 1997 to 2007. 'Noises' is a verb here, as in 'noises abroad'.
explanation.definitionFit: To blare is to make a loud harsh sound, so blares works as a verb meaning trumpets or noises.

clue.text: Worms left rotten cheese

indicators.note: something rotten has decayed out of shape, so these letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Maggots are left in some decaying cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' and 'rotten' read as a verb and an adjective, but give a letter and a signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeches are segmented bloodsucking annelids, a kind of worm in the zoological sense.

clue.text: Argue with Head of Theology, an austere type

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, which alone is kept

blocks.note: spar means to argue or box

explanation.surface: An austere person squabbles with the head of the divinity faculty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An' does double duty: it supplies two letters of the wordplay and also introduces the definition 'austere type'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient Sparta's citizens were famed for frugal, rigorous living, so a spartan is someone of severe simplicity.

clue.text: He's heard novel is to be rewritten

indicators.note: novel means new, so these letters come out in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A writer learns that their book needs another draft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book but is the signal to rearrange 'He's heard'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rehashed means reworked from old material with little change, so a revised text is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Lascar at sea is a rogue

indicators.note: at sea means confused and adrift, so these letters are muddled

explanation.surface: An Indian sailor out on the ocean turns out to be a villain.
explanation.walkthrough: A lascar was a sailor from the Indian subcontinent; 'at sea' fits him perfectly in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A rascal is a mischievous or dishonest person, a synonym for a scoundrel.

clue.text: Rough sport

blocks.note: first meaning: harsh and dry, as of a cough
second meaning: riding a horse for pleasure

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a description of rugby; 'hacking' in British usage is leisurely horse riding.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacking cough is a rough, harsh one, and hacking is also recreational riding in the countryside.

clue.text: Dead excited, texting endlessly about first of concerts

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is dropped
the first of a word is its opening letter alone
excited means stirred up, so these letters are agitated into a new order
about means surrounding, so the shuffled letters go round the single one

explanation.surface: A fan, thrilled to bits, is frantically texting about the first of the gigs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead excited' reads as slang for very excited, but 'Dead' is the definition and 'excited' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An extinct species has died out completely, so it is gone for good.

clue.text: Starts to understand a path to awareness at last

indicators.note: at last points to a word's final letter, which alone is kept

blocks.note: a way is a path or route

explanation.surface: A spiritual guide promising first steps on the road to enlightenment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts' reads as a verb but is a plural noun: quick departures.
explanation.definitionFit: A getaway is a start, especially a fast one, as when a car or runner pulls away.

clue.text: Trainee soldiers set out after villain

indicators.note: set out means laid out in a new way, so these letters are rearranged
one piece follows the other in the answer

blocks.note: a cad is a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: Young recruits go off in pursuit of a criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: A cad is an old-fashioned British word for a man who behaves dishonourably.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadets are young people training to become officers in the armed forces or police.

clue.text: Indian city's Hindu leaders supporting delegate

indicators.note: the leaders of a word are its front letters, so only those are kept
in a down entry, a piece supporting another sits below it

blocks.note: del. is a standard abbreviation for delegate
taken as written; only its first two letters survive

explanation.surface: Leaders of the Hindu community in an Indian city back a delegate.
explanation.walkthrough: The leaders here are the first two letters of 'Hindu', placed beneath the abbreviation for delegate.
explanation.definitionFit: Delhi is the major city in northern India that contains the national capital, New Delhi.

clue.text: Fellow with broken mast is to come ashore somewhere in the Indian Ocean

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so these letters are put back in a new order

blocks.note: to land is to come ashore

explanation.surface: A shipwrecked man with a snapped mast struggles onto a beach in the Indian Ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow' just means a man, so any man's name will do; the crossing letters pin it down.
explanation.definitionFit: Christmas Island is an Australian territory south of Java, out in the eastern Indian Ocean.

clue.text: Anne is going round Italian city

definitions.note: the city is now usually spelt Siena; sienna is the earth pigment named after it

indicators.note: letters going round are swirled about and land in a different order

explanation.surface: Anne is touring a city in Tuscany.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tuscan city is normally spelt Siena with one N; the older English form with two survives in the colour name.
explanation.definitionFit: Siena is a Tuscan hill town, and the setter uses the older English spelling also given to the pigment.

clue.text: I get so annoyed seeing self-centred person

indicators.note: an annoyed person is ruffled and disturbed, so these letters are stirred up

explanation.surface: Someone complains of being irritated by a vain, selfish acquaintance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Annoyed' sits in the surface as a feeling, but signals that 'I get so' is to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An egoist puts their own interests first, a synonym for a selfish or self-absorbed individual.
